title: Mimic
summary: A control dashboard for a robotic arm that copies your hand.

meta.label: STATUS
meta.value: Designed in Figma, UI being coded

meta.label: TEAM
meta.value: Product designer on a robotics team at HackGT 13 (Georgia Tech). My teammates built the arm and the hand tracking.

meta.label: TOOLS
meta.value: Figma and React. Hand tracking from a webcam, built by my teammates.
meta.checkNote: which hand tracking model did your team use?

blocks.text: Mimic is a robotic arm you control with your hand. Move your hand in front of a camera and the arm (MIMIC-V1) follows: left and right to rotate, up and down to raise and lower, pinch to grip and release.

That is a fun idea and a slightly scary one. When your hand is the controller, the operator has to know three things at a glance: is it seeing my hand, what does the arm think I am telling it, and how do I stop it right now?

I was the product designer on a robotics team at HackGT 13, at Georgia Tech. My teammates built the arm and the hand tracking. I designed the dashboard that answers those three questions, and on Sep 26, 2026 I started turning it into code.

The operator is whoever stands in front of the camera. At the hackathon that was me and my teammates. In a demo it is someone trying the arm for the first time. Both need to see at a glance whether the arm is listening to them.

One light desktop dashboard. The live camera feed, with a hand skeleton drawn on it, shows tracking. The current gesture and a control mapping card show what the arm thinks you want. Pause Control and Emergency Stop run full width along the bottom.

blocks.caption: 12 seconds. The live camera feed, the current gesture, the control mapping, and the Emergency Stop.
The final dashboard: camera feed, MIMIC-V1 arm view, current gesture, control mapping, telemetry, and the two stop buttons.

blocks.text: Sync quality, latency, and FPS sit in a telemetry card with small trend lines. A row of chips in the header shows the camera source, the robot connection, sync quality, and a live session timer.
Robotics dashboards are almost always dark. It looks technical. But this screen has to make a live camera feed, a robot render, and a red emergency button all read instantly.

Side by side, the light version gave the cards clearer edges, let the camera feed and the white robot render stand on their own, and made the red Emergency Stop the loudest thing on screen. It also stays readable on a bright projector, which is where a demo actually happens.
Operators need status, but it was showing up in three places at once: header chips, a five-card status column, and the telemetry card.

I tried chips and the column together, then the column alone, then chips alone. Chips alone won. The camera feed got the space back and became noticeably wider, which matters because the feed is how the operator checks that their hand is being tracked. Nothing was lost, since latency and sync already live in telemetry.

before.caption: Before: status column beside the feed

after.caption: After: status moved into the header chips

blocks.text: Saying the same thing three times does not make it clearer. It makes the operator hunt for which one is current. In the same pass I cut the side navigation from six icons to three.

Everything else on this dashboard changed between versions. The stop buttons did not. Pause Control ("temporarily stop sending gesture commands") and Emergency Stop ("immediately halt all robotic arm movement") are in every version, starting with the wireframe.

In the final they are the largest targets on screen, full width at the bottom, with the consequence written on the button. When something goes wrong nobody reads, so the difference between pausing and halting has to be clear from color and words alone.

blocks.caption: Bottom edge of the final dashboard: telemetry, then Pause Control and Emergency Stop.

blocks.text: I would also map the stop to the Space bar, so nobody has to aim a mouse in a hurry.

items.title: Keeping every version was the best call.
items.text: Because I never overwrote a frame, I can show when the status column appeared, moved, and left, and why.

items.title: Removing things is a design skill.
items.text: My biggest improvement between versions was deleting a whole column, not adding a feature.

items.title: Design files are inputs to code.
items.text: Going from frame to code is much smoother when the frame is organized. Naming layers like telemetry-capsules, gesture-card, and button-stop paid off.

blocks.text: The coded version is not finished. For now the camera feed, hand tracking, robot connection, and telemetry run on sample data, so I can get the layout and every state right before wiring it to the real arm, an SO-ARM101 my team used at HackGT 13. Mimic is where my design work meets the physical world: a confusing screen here does not just slow someone down. It moves a robot.

items.text: Design the states I have not drawn yet: hand lost, robot disconnected, high latency, and the screen right after an emergency stop.
Finish the coded version and connect it to live data.
Watch someone who has never seen it and time how long they take to find the stop.
